title: Alice in Wonderland
author: Lewis Carroll
ru: Девочка Алиса падает в кроличью нору и попадает в странную страну, где всё наоборот.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. Down the Rabbit Hole
chapters.text:
Alice was sitting by the river with her sister, and she was bored. Her sister was reading a book. Alice looked at it. There were no pictures in it and no conversations.

“What is the use of a book without pictures or conversations?” she thought.

It was a hot afternoon, and Alice felt sleepy. Then suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran past her.

A rabbit? That was nothing special. But this rabbit said, “Oh dear! Oh dear! I'm going to be late!” Then he took a watch out of his waistcoat pocket, looked at it, and hurried on.

A rabbit with a pocket? And a watch? Alice jumped up and ran across the field after him. She was just in time to see him go down a big rabbit hole under a tree. A second later, Alice went down after him. She didn't stop to think about how to get out again.

The hole went straight down, like a well. Alice fell, and fell, and fell. But she fell very slowly, so she had time to look around. The walls were covered with cupboards and shelves, with maps and pictures here and there. As she went past, she took a jar from a shelf. It said ORANGE MARMALADE. She opened it. Empty! She didn't want to drop it on somebody's head, so she put it back on a shelf lower down.

“After this,” she thought, “falling down the stairs at home will be easy!”

Down, down, down. Was it never going to stop?

“How far down am I now?” she said out loud. “Maybe I'm near the centre of the Earth!”

Then — bump! She landed on a pile of sticks and dry leaves. She wasn't hurt at all. She jumped to her feet and looked around. Far ahead, at the end of a long passage, the White Rabbit was hurrying away.

“Oh, my ears and whiskers,” he said, “how late it's getting!”

Alice ran after him. But when she turned the corner, the Rabbit was gone. She was in a long, low hall, and all around her there were doors.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Pool of Tears
chapters.text:
All the doors were locked. Alice walked sadly up and down the hall. How was she ever going to get out?

Then she saw a small glass table with a tiny golden key on it. Behind a curtain she found a little door, only forty centimetres high. She tried the key, and it fitted! She opened the door and looked through. On the other side was a beautiful garden, full of bright flowers and cool fountains. But the door was far too small. She couldn't even get her head through it.

She went back to the table. Now there was a little bottle on it with a label: DRINK ME.

Alice was a careful girl. She looked for the word POISON. No, it wasn't there. So she drank it. It tasted of cherry tart, roast chicken and hot buttered toast, all at the same time.

“What a strange feeling!” she said. She was getting smaller and smaller — until she was only twenty-five centimetres tall. Now she could go through the little door! But oh no — the key was still on the table, high above her head. She tried to climb up the table leg, but it was too slippery. In the end she sat down and cried.

Then she saw a little cake under the table. On it, in beautiful letters, were the words EAT ME. So she ate it.

“Curiouser and curiouser!” she cried. She began to grow again, up and up, until her head hit the ceiling. Now she was three metres tall! She picked up the key and ran to the garden door. But now she had to lie on the floor, and she could only look through it with one eye. Poor Alice! She began to cry again. Her tears were enormous, and soon there was a big pool of salty water all over the floor.

Then she heard the sound of little feet. It was the White Rabbit, in his best clothes, with white gloves in one hand and a fan in the other.

“Please, sir—” Alice began.

The Rabbit jumped, dropped the gloves and the fan, and ran away into the dark.

It was very hot in the hall, so Alice picked up the fan and began to fan herself. And — what was happening? — she was getting smaller again! Smaller, smaller... and then splash! She was up to her chin in salt water. She was swimming in a sea of her own tears.

And something was swimming next to her. It was a mouse.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Advice from a Caterpillar
chapters.text:
Alice swam to the side of the pool and climbed out onto the grass. The hall and the doors were gone! The mouse and lots of other wet animals climbed out too, but soon they all went away. Alice was alone, and she was still very small. Even the grass was taller than she was.

She walked into a wood. Next to her there was a big mushroom, so she stood on her toes and looked over the top.

A large blue caterpillar was sitting on it with his arms folded. He was smoking a long pipe, very slowly, and he didn't say a word.

At last he took the pipe out of his mouth. “Who are YOU?” he asked in a sleepy voice.

“I'm not sure, sir,” said Alice. “I knew who I was when I got up this morning. But then I changed so many times!”

“What do you mean?” said the Caterpillar. “Explain yourself!”

“I can't explain myself,” said Alice, “because I'm not myself, you see.”

“I don't see,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, it's very confusing to be so many different sizes in one day,” said Alice.

“It isn't,” said the Caterpillar.

“Maybe not for you,” said Alice. “But one day you're going to turn into a butterfly. Won't that feel a little strange?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, it feels very strange to ME,” said Alice.

“You!” said the Caterpillar. “Who are YOU?”

They were back at the beginning! Alice turned to go.

“Come back!” called the Caterpillar. “I have something important to say.”

Alice came back.

“Keep your temper,” said the Caterpillar.

“Is that all?” asked Alice, trying hard not to get angry.

“No.” He smoked his pipe for a long, long time. Then he said, “So what size do you want to be?”

“Oh, a little bigger, please,” said Alice. “Eight centimetres is a terrible height.”

“It's a very good height!” said the Caterpillar angrily. He sat up very straight. He was exactly eight centimetres tall.

Then he got down from the mushroom and crawled away into the grass. “One side will make you taller,” he said, “and the other side will make you shorter.”

“One side of WHAT?” thought Alice.

“Of the mushroom,” said the Caterpillar. Could he hear her thoughts? And then he was gone.

Alice broke off a piece from each side of the mushroom. Now she could choose her size — big or small, whenever she liked. “That's going to be very useful!” she thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Cheshire Cat
chapters.text:
Alice ate a little from one piece of mushroom, then a little from the other, until she was her normal height again. It felt strange, but nice.

Soon she came to a small house in the wood. The door was open, so she went in.

The kitchen was full of smoke. An ugly old Duchess — a very important lady — was sitting in the middle of the room with a baby in her arms, and the cook was making soup — with much too much pepper in it. Alice was sneezing, the Duchess was sneezing, and the baby was sneezing and screaming at the same time. Only the cook and a big cat by the fire weren't sneezing. The cat was smiling from ear to ear.

“Why does your cat smile like that?” asked Alice.

“It's a Cheshire cat,” said the Duchess. “That's why. PIG!”

Alice jumped. But the Duchess was talking to the baby, not to her.

Then the cook began to throw things at the Duchess and the baby — pans, plates, dishes, everything. The Duchess didn't even look up. “Here! You can hold it for a bit!” she said, and she threw the baby to Alice. Then she went off to play croquet with the Queen.

Alice carried the baby outside. It was a very strange baby. Its nose was turning up, and its eyes were getting smaller and smaller. Then it grunted, like a pig.

Alice looked down. It was a pig! She put it on the ground, and it ran happily away into the trees.

“It was a very ugly baby,” thought Alice, “but it makes a rather nice pig.”

Then she saw the Cheshire Cat again. It was sitting on a branch of a tree, still smiling.

“Excuse me,” said Alice, a little shyly, “which way should I go from here?”

“That depends on where you want to get to,” said the Cat.

“I don't really care where—” said Alice.

“Then it doesn't matter which way you go,” said the Cat. “A Hatter lives over THERE.” It waved one paw. “And a March Hare lives over THERE. You can visit either of them. They're both mad.”

“But I don't want to be with mad people,” said Alice.

“Oh, you can't help that,” said the Cat. “We're all mad here. I'm mad. You're mad.”

“How do you know I'm mad?” asked Alice.

“You must be,” said the Cat, “or you wouldn't be here.”

Then it slowly disappeared. First the tail went, then the body, then the head. In the end only the smile was left, hanging in the air.

“Well!” thought Alice. “I know lots of cats without smiles. But a smile without a cat? That's the strangest thing in the world!”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. A Mad Tea Party
chapters.text:
Alice decided to visit the March Hare. Soon she saw his house. It had chimneys like long ears and a roof made of fur. Under a tree in front of it there was a long table. The March Hare and the Hatter were having tea. A Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep, and they were using him as a cushion for their elbows.

The table was very big, but the three of them were all sitting at one corner. “No room! No room!” they shouted when they saw Alice.

“There's LOTS of room!” said Alice, and she sat down in a big armchair at the end of the table.

“Have some wine,” said the March Hare kindly.

Alice looked all round the table. There was only tea on it. “I don't see any wine,” she said.

“There isn't any,” said the March Hare.

“Then it wasn't very polite to offer it,” said Alice crossly.

“It wasn't very polite to sit down without an invitation,” said the March Hare.

The Hatter looked at Alice for a long time. Then he asked, “Why is a raven like a writing desk?”

“Oh good, a riddle!” thought Alice. “I think I can guess that,” she said out loud. She thought and thought, but in the end she gave up. “What's the answer?”

“I have no idea,” said the Hatter.

“Me neither,” said the March Hare.

Alice sighed. “Why ask riddles with no answers? It's a waste of time.”

“Time!” said the Hatter sadly. “Time and I had an argument last March. And now he never does anything for me. It's always six o'clock now — always tea time. We never have time to wash the cups.”

“So when your cups are dirty, you just move to the next place?” asked Alice.

“Exactly,” said the Hatter.

“But what happens when you get back to the beginning?”

“Let's talk about something else,” said the March Hare quickly. “Have some more tea.”

“There's no tea in my cup,” said Alice, “so I can't take MORE.”

“You mean you can't take LESS,” said the Hatter. “It's very easy to take MORE than nothing.”

That was too much for Alice. She got up and walked away. When she looked back, the Hatter and the March Hare were trying to put the Dormouse into the teapot.

“That was the silliest tea party of my whole life!” she said.

Then she noticed a door in the trunk of a tree. A door in a tree? “Well, everything is strange today,” thought Alice. “I'll just go in.” She went in — and she was back in the long hall with all the doors! This time she knew what to do. She took the little golden key, ate some mushroom until she was small, and opened the little door. And there, at last, was the beautiful garden.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Queen of Hearts
chapters.text:
Near the entrance to the garden stood a big rose tree. Its roses were white, but three gardeners were busy painting them red. The gardeners were very strange: they were flat, with hands and feet at the corners — just like playing cards.

“Excuse me,” said Alice, “why are you painting those roses?”

“Well, miss,” said one of them quietly, “this should be a RED rose tree. We planted a white one by mistake. If the Queen sees it, she'll cut our heads off! So we—”

“The Queen! The Queen!” someone shouted, and the three gardeners threw themselves flat on their faces.

First came ten soldiers, then the royal children, then the guests — all cards. The White Rabbit was there too, talking very fast and smiling at everyone. Last of all came the King and Queen of Hearts.

The Queen stopped in front of Alice. “What's your name, child?”

“My name is Alice, Your Majesty,” said Alice politely. But she thought, “They're only a pack of cards. I don't need to be afraid of them!”

The Queen looked at the rose tree. Then she looked at the gardeners on the ground. “Off with their heads!” she screamed.

The soldiers came for the gardeners, but Alice quickly hid them in a big flowerpot. The soldiers looked around for a minute or two, then marched away.

“Can you play croquet?” shouted the Queen.

“Yes!” shouted Alice.

“Come on, then!”

It was the strangest game of croquet in the world. In croquet you hit a ball with a long hammer, and the ball must go through little arches. But here the balls were live hedgehogs, and the hammers were live flamingos! The soldiers bent over to make the arches. Every time Alice tried to hit her hedgehog, her flamingo turned its long neck and looked up into her face. She couldn't stop laughing. And when she was ready at last, the hedgehog was walking away.

Everybody played at the same time, and everybody argued. The Queen got angrier and angrier, and about once a minute she shouted “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!”

Then Alice saw something strange in the air: a smile. Then two eyes. Then a whole head. It was the Cheshire Cat.

“How's the game going?” asked the Cat.

“They don't play fair at all,” said Alice. “And there aren't any rules.”

The King came over and looked at the Cat's head. “I don't like the look of it at all,” he said. “My dear, please take this cat away!”

“Off with its head!” said the Queen, without even turning round.

“You can't cut off a head when there's no body,” said the executioner — the man with the big axe.

“Anything with a head can lose it!” said the King.

“Do something NOW, or I'll cut off EVERYBODY'S head!” screamed the Queen.

And while they were all arguing, the Cat's head slowly disappeared.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Who Stole the Tarts?
chapters.text:
“The trial is beginning!” someone shouted, and everybody ran.

The King and Queen of Hearts were sitting on their thrones, with a big crowd of birds, animals and cards around them. The Knave of Hearts stood in front of them in chains. Twelve animals sat in a box at the side of the room. They were the jury. In the middle of the room there was a table with a big plate of tarts on it. They looked so good that Alice felt hungry.

The White Rabbit blew his trumpet and read:

“The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts,
All on a summer day:
The Knave of Hearts, he stole those tarts,
And took them quite away!”

The first witness was the Hatter. He came in with a teacup in one hand and some bread and butter in the other. He was so nervous that he bit a piece out of his teacup instead of the bread. “You can go,” said the King, and the Hatter ran out — without his shoes.

Just then, Alice felt something strange. She began to grow again — bigger and bigger.

“Call the next witness!” said the King. The White Rabbit looked at his list and read out in a high little voice, “Alice!”

“Here!” cried Alice. She jumped up — and because she was so big now, her skirt knocked over the jury box, and all twelve animals fell out onto the floor.

“What do you know about this business?” asked the King.

“Nothing,” said Alice.

Then the King read from his book: “Rule Forty-two. All persons more than a mile high must leave the court.”

Everybody looked at Alice.

“I'm not a mile high,” said Alice.

“You are,” said the King.

“Nearly two miles high,” said the Queen.

“Well, I'm not going,” said Alice. “That isn't a real rule. You just made it up!”

“It's the oldest rule in the book,” said the King.

“Then it should be Number One,” said Alice.

The King went white and quickly closed his book.

“Now, the jury must decide,” said the King. “Did the Knave steal the tarts?”

“No!” said the Queen. “Punishment first — decision later!”

“What nonsense!” said Alice loudly.

“Be quiet!” said the Queen, turning purple.

“I won't!” said Alice.

“Off with her head!” the Queen shouted at the top of her voice. Nobody moved.

“Who cares about you?” said Alice. She was her real size again — much bigger than any card. “You're nothing but a pack of cards!”

At that, the whole pack flew up into the air and came down on top of her. Alice gave a little scream and tried to push them away —

— and she was lying by the river, with her head in her sister's lap. Her sister was gently brushing some dry leaves off her face.

“Wake up, Alice dear!” said her sister. “What a long sleep!”

“Oh, I had such a curious dream!” said Alice. And she told her sister all about it: the White Rabbit, the Caterpillar, the Cheshire Cat, the mad tea party and the Queen of Hearts.

Her sister listened and smiled. And for a moment, she too could hear the little feet of the White Rabbit in the grass.
